section: What to do when you’re uncertain?

What to do when you’re uncertain?

Turn up the gain. Enroll help. “Are we certain this is asystole?”. If in doubt, shock.

title: Pulse Check Decisions
text:
What is the big picture?
Only a few things really matter

If they don’t have a pulse, someone is performing high quality compressions with NO significant breaks

Limit pauses (position changes, pulse checks, intubation, Lucas)

Shock early when they have a shockable rhythm

title: Pulse Check Decisions
text:

Be the point person







Do not move from your position. Don’t do it!

title: Effective Leadership Skills
text:
Step 2: Collaborate, Share Info:
Invite suggestions with a constructive tone
Try:

Think out loud: “Wide QRS, but rhythm is irregular”
Summarize: “MAP is OK, I think this is AFib, so…”
Encourage: “Good thought, yes…”

Why? The team has a lot of context-specific experience

title: Effective Leadership Skills
text:
Collaboration includes nursing context
When you arrive, the bedside nurse or outreach nurse may know the trajectory better than anyone in the room.
Ask early:

“What changed, what have you already tried, and what are you most worried about?”

Then make the plan explicit.

text:
The scenarios are designed for in-person practice with the Zoll. Use the public slides for learner review; facilitator-specific prompts belong in the instructor guide.
Each case now includes a brief resident/nurse-team interface prompt: who has bedside context, what the resident should ask, and how the plan should be closed-looped.


Case 1
Pulseless patient with severe metabolic derangements. Focus: asystole versus fine VF, the less-bad error when uncertain, and using nurse recorder/timekeeper input during rhythm checks.
Open case


Case 2
Pulseless VF/VT physiology with post-ROSC ECG decision-making. Focus: first shock, cause search, and closed-loop coordination with defibrillator/medication roles.
Open case


Case 3
Polymorphic VT/TdP after QT-prolonging medications. Focus: pulseless defibrillation versus unstable cardioversion versus stable magnesium, plus pharmacy/nursing medication-history input.

Case 5
Bradycardia with hypotension and confusion. Focus: complete heart block, pacing pads, transcutaneous pacing setup, sedation planning, and shared preparation with bedside nursing.

title: 2026 Code Blue and Rapid Response Seminar
text:
Why This Course Exists
Code Blue and Rapid Response leadership is not just algorithm recall. The resident leader has to make the room work: claim the leader role, make roles visible, keep communication psychologically safe, integrate bedside expertise, and escalate resources before the response stalls.
Stakeholders from Code Blue and Rapid Response teams, including senior residents, nurses, respiratory therapists, and quality leads, identified four recurring hazards during resident-led responses:

Unclear team leadership, which can cause role confusion, low psychological safety, and decreased collaboration. (Steinbach et al. 2024)
Failure to cardiovert or defibrillate shockable rhythms.
Delayed critical decisions, including calling for help, initial stabilization, and transport to ICU.
Poorly defined collaboration between residents and bedside nurses, nurse-led rapid response teams, or critical care outreach teams.

This seminar targets those hazards through brief micro-skills, discussion, hands-on scenarios, and interprofessional scripts that can be used during real events.

3. Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams

4. Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
Practice deciding when a rapid is becoming a code, what resources are needed, where the patient should go, how to hand off, and how to debrief.

title: Resources
text: Quick reference materials for Code Blue and Rapid Response leadership.

title: Resources
text:
Key Points

Establish the leader early. Try: “I’m Joe/Jane Doe, the resident on the code team. Who is running this code/RRT?” or “Can I take over?”
Ask for the nursing/outreach 30-second story. Try: “What changed, what have you already tried, and what are you most worried about?”
Stay at the foot of the bed when leading. Do not drift into tasks that pull you out of room management.
Keep the big picture visible. For an RRT, ask whether this is becoming a code or whether the patient needs ICU. For a code, protect high-quality compressions and shock early if shockable.
Close the loop before leaving. Name disposition, orders, ownership, and debrief plan.

title: Resources
text:
Nurse-Team Huddle Script


“Let’s huddle for 30 seconds. I’m running the rapid unless someone else is. Bedside nurse, what changed? Outreach, what are you worried about? My working problem is [problem]. Our immediate plan is [plan]. If [trigger] happens, call a code.”


Use this when nursing or outreach is already actively managing the patient. The goal is not to slow the response; it is to prevent parallel, conflicting plans.

section: Code blue: when do you stop?
text:
Code blue: when do you stop?
Young patient. Seems like a PE.
She has been in PEA at each pulse check.
Resuscitation has been going on for 40 minutes.
When do you stop?

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Factors that change duration
Consider:

pre-arrest state
witnessed vs unwitnessed
monitored vs unmonitored
likely reversible cause
rhythm trajectory
EtCO2 and physiologic signs
family/surrogate context when available

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Family presence

Use judgement, delegate attention, and try to include when possibleUse judgment.
Delegate attention.
Try to include when possible and safe.

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
section: How to end an unsuccessful attempted resuscitation
text:
How to end an unsuccessful attempted resuscitation
Try:

“Does anyone have ideas we have not tried?”


“We are going to stop CPR at the next check unless the rhythm changes.”

Then:

thank team members
name death pronouncement workflow
assign family communication
set a time and location to debrief

title: Escalation, Disposition, and Closure
text:
Summary

Escalate early when the room is not safe enough.
Know what resources each site can bring.
Decide disposition before drifting away.
End with handoff, ownership, and debrief.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Working with nurse-led response teams
Learners will practice:

Clarifying who is leading
Getting the nursing 30-second story
Stating the working problem and first plan
Using the nurse/outreach lead as a safety partner
Closing the loop on orders, disposition, and ownership

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Why this matters
In many deteriorating-patient events, the bedside nurse or critical care outreach nurse has already:

recognized the trajectory
started stabilization
gathered unit-specific context
called for help
anticipated what the patient may need next

You need that information early.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Case start
You are called to an RRT.
A critical care outreach nurse and bedside nurse are already in the room. The patient is tachypneic, newly confused, and on escalating oxygen.
The primary intern is present but quiet. The charge nurse is trying to find the primary team.
What is your first sentence?

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Move 1: Name the leadership state
Try:

“I’m [name], the medicine resident/code resident. Who is currently coordinating this response?”

Then choose one:

“Okay, I’ll run the rapid.”
“Can I take over?”
“Okay, how can I help?”

Do not leave leadership ambiguous.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
section: Move 2: Ask for the nursing 30-second story
text:
Move 2: Ask for the nursing 30-second story
Ask the bedside or outreach nurse:

“Can I get the 30-second story: what changed, what have you already tried, and what are you most worried about?”

Listen for:

trajectory
trigger for concern
therapies already attempted
missing resources
whether this is about to become a code

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
section: Move 3: Say the working problem and first plan
text:
Move 3: Say the working problem and first plan
Make your thinking public:

“I think this is acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with possible shock. In the next two minutes: nonrebreather, ABG/VBG, CXR, two IVs, lactate, cultures, and call ICU now.”

Then assign roles.
If the plan changes, say so out loud.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
section: Move 4: Use the nurse/outreach lead as a safety partner
text:
Move 4: Use the nurse/outreach lead as a safety partner
Ask:

“What am I missing?”


“What worries you most right now?”


“What resources do we need that are not in the room?”

If the nurse says the patient is unsafe, slow down and reassess.

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Move 5: Close the loop
Before leaving, make these explicit:

disposition: floor, ICU, code, procedure, transfer
orders: who is placing them
ownership: who is managing the patient now
communication: who calls family / attending / ICU
debrief: when and where

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Practice script
Use this in the room:

“Let’s huddle for 30 seconds. I’m running the rapid unless someone else is. Bedside nurse, what changed? Outreach, what are you worried about? My working problem is [problem]. Our immediate plan is [plan]. If [trigger] happens, call a code.”

title: Working with Nurse-Led Response Teams
text:
Summary

Name leadership.
Ask for the nursing 30-second story.
State the working problem and first plan.
Treat the nurse/outreach lead as a safety partner.
Close the loop before leaving.
